html:
The Zapotec state was centred on the hilltop city of Monte Albán, which ruled the Valley of Oaxaca in southern Mexico from about 500 BCE until it faded around 850 CE.

Monte Albán was founded on a levelled mountain top above the valley floor, a site that was easy to defend but had no water of its own. It was one of the first true cities in Mesoamerica. Its great plaza is lined with temples, palaces and a ball court. Early stone slabs there, called the "Danzantes", show sprawled figures who were probably captives, along with glyphs that are among the oldest writing in Mesoamerica. The Zapotecs also used the 260-day ritual calendar shared across the region.

At its height, the city ruled most of the Oaxaca valley and beyond. It kept close ties with Teotihuacan: carved stones at Monte Albán show envoys from that city, and Zapotec migrants had their own neighbourhood in Teotihuacan. Like Teotihuacan, Monte Albán was abandoned as a capital in the centuries after 700, and power split among smaller valley towns.

The Zapotec people did not vanish with the city. Zapotec kingdoms faced the Aztecs and then the Spanish, and Zapotec is still spoken in Oaxaca today. Benito Juárez, president of Mexico in the 1800s, was Zapotec. Mesoamerica's other early civilisation, the Olmecs, had faded just as Monte Albán rose.
sum: The Zapotec state was centred on the hilltop city of Monte Albán, which ruled the Valley of Oaxaca in southern Mexico from about 500 BCE until it faded around 850 CE.
